entities.name: Koutoubia Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Koutoubia Mosque (Mosque of the Booksellers) in Marrakech, Morocco, built by Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min between 1147-1158 CE, is the largest mosque in Morocco, the model for the Giralda minaret in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat, and the architectural prototype that defined Moorish mosque aesthetics across the western Islamic world. The 70-meter Koutoubia minaret — with its decorated arched windows, intricate carved plasterwork, and four copper balls (jamur) crowning the top — is the defining landmark of Marrakech and the standard against which all subsequent North African minarets were measured.

The Koutoubia's name ('kutubiyyin' — booksellers) reflects its original surroundings: the medieval book market of Marrakech clustered around the mosque, making it a center of Islamic learning as well as prayer. The mosque was built on the site of an earlier Almoravid palace — Almohad doctrine required demolishing Almoravid buildings as religiously impure — and an excavated first Koutoubia mosque. The current mosque is actually the second building on the site.

The minaret's architectural influence is extraordinary: Abd al-Rahman I's grandson (Abd al-Mu'min) used the same proportional system and decorative vocabulary for the Giralda (Seville, begun 1184) and the Hassan Tower (Rabat, begun 1195) — creating a deliberate architectural unity across the Almohad Empire from Morocco to Andalusia. The three minarets represent the apogee of Almohad architectural achievement. The Koutoubia minaret's proportions (1:5 base-to-height ratio) and the decorative panel (shebka) system became canonical for Moroccan mosque architecture for the next 800 years.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Koutoubia Mosque's minaret — the direct architectural prototype for both the Giralda (Seville) and Hassan Tower (Rabat) — created a deliberate architectural unity across the Almohad Empire that makes it the single most influential building in the formation of western Islamic architectural identity.
